item.title: In-plane diffusion, spurious drift and a physics-structured gap predictor for a free colloidal pair
item.description: arXiv:2611.17508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When the diffusivity of a Brownian particle depends on position, its mean displacement acquires a noise-induced (spurious) drift whose magnitude is set by the stochastic convention $\alpha$. We ask how much of this physics can be extracted from a pair of 1.95 $\mu$m polystyrene spheres released from blinking holographic optical tweezers at five bath temperatures between 2 and 40 $^\circ$C. The single-sphere diffusivity inside the pair stays between 0.093 and 0.098 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, whereas the Stokes-Einstein value for water rises from 0.126 to 0.361 $\mu$m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; an isolated sphere reproduces the deficit, which is therefore not a pair effect. From the measured gap-dependent diffusivities $D_\parallel(h)$ and $D_\perp(h)$ we build a Fokker-Planck predictor of the future gap and score it on held-out releases. It recovers the 90% width of the gap distribution up to 800 ms but cannot discriminate between $\alpha = 0$, $1/2$ and $1$, because the $\alpha$-dependent mean shift is an order of magnitude smaller than that width. The ensemble spurious drift is consistent with zero at both ends of the temperature range, and the regression for $\alpha$ never exceeds $R^2 = 0.22$. We therefore present a planar methods baseline and identify the measurements required to resolve $\alpha$.
item.dc:creator: Juan Pablo Staforelli Vivanco, Cristobal Augusto Vald\'es Cruces

item.title: Stress peaks and rupture in star-polymer networks with bidisperse arm lengths
item.description: arXiv:2611.17648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The tensile response of phantom star-polymer networks with bidisperse arm lengths is examined by energy-minimization simulations. Short and long precursors form short-short, short-long, and long-long strands within one end-linked network. The contrast among these strands, composition, functionality, and reaction conversion are varied, and their effects on network rupture are examined. At a large length contrast, two stress peaks appear over part of the composition range. In such realizations, short-short strands carry most of the stress at the first peak, while short-long strands carry most of it after the intervening stress drop. Interesting findings are i) that the peak stretches, including those in double-peak cases, follow composition-dependent master curves when plotted against cycle-rank density, as in monodisperse networks, and ii) that a recently proposed mechanical model describes their cycle-rank dependence, with parameters that vary with composition and arm-length contrast. The parameters differ between the peak series, although their separate determination is limited in some conditions. In addition, the Mark-type improvement of the mechanical properties of the networks by adding a fraction of short strands is discussed. With the implemented FENE force law, the work up to the global stress peak is closer to the long-only value, but an improvement above that reference is not statistically resolved.
item.dc:creator: Yuichi Masubuchi

item.title: Active turbulent flows of dense persistent particles driven at constant velocity
item.description: arXiv:2611.17777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study dense assemblies of self-propelled particles with infinitely persistent active forces, driven at a constant average velocity $V$ along their propulsion directions. Because the velocity $V$ introduces a finite timescale, it plays a role analogous to the shear rate in globally-deformed amorphous solids, and the system approaches a transition analogous to a yielding transition as $V \to 0$. We construct a force-velocity flow curve which is of the Herschel-Bulkley type, with a finite force threshold for flow. As $V$ decreases, the instantaneous velocity field becomes increasingly dominated by rare, localized plastic events, which produce fat tails in the velocity distribution and coexist with a slow, spatially correlated flow of streams and vortices. Many such events must accumulate throughout the system to fully relax its structure, so that the flow patterns reorganize after particles have been driven over a few particle diameters. The spatial extent of these correlated flows grows rapidly as $V$ decreases, and becomes only limited by the finite system size in our simulations. The kinetic energy spectrum displays a robust $k^{-1/2}$ regime also found in self-propelled particles at large but finite persistence times. Approaching the flow threshold thus leads to the same active turbulent state as increasing the persistence time in dense active matter, while displaying both analogies and differences with the yielding transition in sheared glassy materials.
item.dc:creator: Yonglun Jiang, Juliane Klamser, Ludovic Berthier

item.title: Shape of semiflexible polymer chains: L\'evy walks vs. Persistent random walks
item.description: arXiv:2611.17992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The conformational size and shape characteristics of semiflexible polymer chains, modeled via two distinct frameworks: persistent random walks (PRW) and L\'evy walks (LW), are analyzed through numerical simulations. We introduce a mapping that treats the mean jump length $\langle \ell \rangle$ of a L\'evy distribution ($\sim \ell^{-(1+\sigma)}$) as an effective persistence length of the semiflexible polymer chain, controlled by the exponent $\sigma $. While the conformational characteristics of the PRW model statistically exhibit a sharp crossover from flexible coil to the rigid-rod-like behavior in the immediate vicinity of the maximum persistence probability $p \to 1$, the LW model shows a much richer conformational behavior. We obtain the quantitative estimates for universal shape parameters, such as asphericity \(\langle A_3 \rangle\) and prolateness \(\langle S \rangle\), which gradually increase with decreasing parameter $\sigma $ (and thus with an increase of the persistence length), thus supporting previously observed findings for semiflexible polymers. Our results demonstrate the effictiveness of applying L\'evy-walk statistics to capture the universal conformational properties of semiflexible polymer structures.
item.dc:creator: V. Blavatska, Yu. Honchar, Yu. Holovatch

item.title: A Cantilever-Based Method for Probing Adhesion Force and Kinetic Detachment Energy in Cohesive Granular Materials
item.description: arXiv:2611.18021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interparticle adhesion plays a critical role in the flow behavior of cohesive granular materials, yet quantitative characterization at the particle scale remains challenging. Here, we present a cantilever-based method that combines a glass-beam cantilever for force measurements with a novel catapult mode for energy measurements, enabling the determination of both quasi-static detachment force and kinetic detachment energy. Applied to three different cohesive materials: polymer-coated silica particles, wet granular media, and cross-linked poly(2-ethylhexyl acrylate) (PEHA) microparticles, this method reveals a fundamental decoupling between force and energy, suggesting that both quantities are equally critical for characterizing grain properties.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Lajeunesse, Francisco M. Rocha, Denis Dumont, Vincent Bertin, Yoanh Moratille, Nathalie Sintes-Zydowicz, Eric Drockenmuller, Olivier Pouliquen

item.title: Comment on "Kinematic and Rheological Equivalence of Steady Shearing and Planar Extensional Flows"
item.description: arXiv:2611.18048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Reference [Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 144003 (2026)], the authors claim the 'kinematic' and 'rheological' equivalence between simple shear and planar extension. They state that their result holds "for any materially objective constitutive equation." The proposed relation is exact for single-mode constitutive models whose stress is coaxial with a single tensor obeying an evolution equation that depends linearly on the velocity gradient. However, it fails for standard kinetic theories of dilute solutions, e.g. FENE dumbbells, and for the integral tube or K-BKZ models of entangled solutions and melts. Their result is a consequence of the employed closures, not of an underlying equivalence between the flows. Its accuracy for real fluids cannot be inferred from such closed models and instead requires independent validation against measured planar extensional data.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Hillebrand

item.title: A Tissue Vertex Model grounded in Continuum Mechanics
item.description: arXiv:2611.18295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practical modeling of disordered single-layer confluent tissues has relied heavily on the two-dimensional standard vertex model (SVM), which simplifies cell elasticity using an energy functional determined by quadratic dependence of cell area and perimeter values. Realistically, even a coarse-grained cell interior consists of effective continuum materials representing cytoplasm and peripheral cortex, with elastic energy depending on stress and strain fields. It is shown that this energy is analytically tractable for polygonal cell shapes, that its area dependence can be eliminated, that it correlates well with cell perimeter length, and that the perimeter dependence of the correlation is not quadratic. This results in a revised vertex model derived from continuum elasticity whose parameters are predicted from tissue material properties and whose resultant forces are far less strain-dependent than in the SVM.
item.dc:creator: Jairo M. Rojas, Mayisha Z. Nakib, Sascha Hilgenfeldt

item.title: Delay-induced current reversal in traveling activity waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.18341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-propelled particles that regulate their speed based on a response to a local activity source can move with or against a traveling wave of that source depending on their response time. Silica-titania Janus microswimmers, whose UV-controlled speed relaxes with a delay intrinsic to the titania photoconductivity adaptation, carry two independent memory channels: the familiar directional memory dictated by persistent active Brownian motion, and a distinct memory from the speed adaptation. Combining experiments, Langevin simulations, and a moment expansion of the corresponding Fokker-Planck equation, we show that this delayed response to speed adaptation reshapes transport under traveling UV-illumination waves and can even reverse it relative to the direction set by orientational memory alone. In particular, we observe that delay promotes transport in the direction opposite to the traveling activity waves, where, beyond a critical value, the particle current reverses with respect to the wave propagation direction. Crucially, this behavior requires an asymmetric response to the speed adaptation, with an instantaneous rise but a delayed fall upon exposure to time-varying UV light. Theory further shows that this phenomenology is specific to the response asymmetry rather than to the mere presence of a delay, i.e. reversing the asymmetry reverses the effect of the delay on the particle current relative to the wave. We thus establish propulsion-delay asymmetry as a control parameter for directed transport of responsive active particles in traveling activity landscapes.
item.dc:creator: Ueli T\"opfer, Adri\`a Garc\'es, Miguel Chamorro-Burgos, Demian Levis, Alvaro Dom\'inguez, Ignacio Pagonabarraga, Lucio Isa

item.title: Frustrated Interlayer Coupling Creates a Higher-Order Helical Superstructure in a Twist-Bend Smectic Phase
item.description: arXiv:2611.18347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bent liquid-crystalline dimers provide a model system for studying the spontaneous emergence of chirality from achiral molecules. Depending on terminal-chain length, these materials exhibit a competition between heliconical, synclinic, and anticlinic packing tendencies in tilted smectic phases. In short homologues, the tendency to form twist-bend phases dominates, leading to two distinct helical phases: the SmCTB-SH phase, with a helical periodicity of four molecular lengths, and at lower temperatures, a double helical structure - the SmCTB-DH phase, with progressive rotation of the four-layer unit. With increasing terminal chain length, this twist-bend tendency is gradually suppressed, favoring phases with simple synclinic and anticlinic tilt arrangement in successive layers. Remarkably, in the regime where these tendencies become comparable, a new modulated smectic phase, SmCTB-mod develops; a double helical structure in which the internal four-layer unit undergoes a periodic modulation. This additional level of structural organization provides a means of accommodating competing heliconical and synclinic/anticlinic tendencies and produces a characteristic splitting of the resonant x-ray diffraction peaks into four signals symmetrically located around a signal of four-layer periodicity. These results reveal how bent dimers resolve local-packing-mode frustration through complex spontaneous hierarchical structural organization.
item.dc:creator: Abigail Pearson, Damian Pociecha, Magdalena M. Majewska, Nata\v{s}a Vaupoti\v{c}, Rebecca Walker, Ewa Gorecka

item.title: Emergent intercellular contact-force networks shaped by deformability
item.description: arXiv:2611.18414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a numerical study of contact-force organization in dense assemblies of active, deformable cells. Using the Fourier Contour Cell model, which enables efficient simulation of large cell deformations, we investigate how cell deformability and active motility shape spatial organization of intercellular forces. We find that, in the soft liquid regime at intermediate self-propulsion strength, the contact-force distribution becomes bimodal, reflecting the emergence of a distinct population of weak interactions. Persistent-homology analysis further reveals a characteristic force-network structure in which weak tip-tip interactions are enclosed by loops of strong side-side interactions. Simulations with elongated but non-deformable cells demonstrate that both the bimodal force distribution and the associated network motif require cell deformability rather than elongated cell shape per se. Furthermore, introducing a curvature constraint shows that local cell curvature regulates the strength of weak tip-tip interactions. Together, these results demonstrate that cell deformability and local geometric constraints can organize force transmission across dense active cellular assemblies.
item.dc:creator: Koshi Yoshida, Nen Saito, Shuji Ishihara, Kaoru Sugimura

item.title: Deformation Kinetics of Charged Nanoclusters via Surface Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2611.17514v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-temperature charged nanoclusters deform, primarily via surface diffusion, when surface electrostatic stresses and surface tension stresses are not balanced. We derive an analytical model for the kinetics of this process, based on the cluster size, net charge, surface tension, local curvature, temperature, and diffusivity. The model predicts the deformation time when either surface tension or electrostatic stress dominates, leading respectively to the collapse or elongation of the cluster. Comparison with molecular dynamics simulations of ice nanoclusters with solvated electrons shows quantitative agreement with a single fitted parameter. The model can predict the deformation kinetics of charged nanoclusters in atmospheric aerosols and complex plasmas.
item.dc:creator: Efstratios M. Kritikos, William A. Goddard III, Paul M. Bellan

item.title: Influence of transverse oscillatory shear on the viscous fingering instability
item.description: arXiv:2611.17551v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Oscillatory shear can delay the onset of viscous fingering. In addition, uniaxial translational shear also breaks the symmetry of the resulting pattern so that the interface evolves differently depending on its direction of propagation relative to the shear axis. We observe a delayed fingering onset and reduced subsequent finger growth rate for all directions as shear speed or amplitude increases. However, shear widens fingers growing in the direction perpendicular to shear and elongates those in the parallel directions. After onset, neighboring fingers in the perpendicular directions can reconnect near their base when the shear amplitude exceeds approximately five times the excess linear finger wavelength at the onset. Concentration profiles reveal smoother azimuthal edges and overlapping structures behind the tips. These observations show that shear smears individual fingers and connects neighboring ones. This correlates lateral fingering interactions with radial propagation.
item.dc:creator: Zhaoning Liu

item.title: Physics-informed digital twin and onboard control of a brainbot for intelligent active matter
item.description: arXiv:2511.00384v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Establishing adaptive particles that sense their state, anticipate their evolution, and compute control inputs onboard has been a major challenge in non-equilibrium physics. We address this challenge by realizing an autonomous brainbot, building on a recently developed programmable bristlebot. First, we construct a physics-informed digital twin of the device, based on a kinematic model that reproduces measured trajectory statistics and generates long, statistically faithful synthetic trajectories. The kinematics forms the foundation for implementing onboard model predictive control (MPC), enabling autonomous trajectory tracking, demonstrated by accurate execution of a non-trivial target path. This provides a proof of principle for a brainbot that senses its state, predicts its evolution, and computes control inputs onboard, unlike conventional active particles with fixed motility, thereby transforming the brainbot into an agentic physical entity. By integrating physical modeling, data-driven parameter identification, and control into a unified framework, our approach provides a scalable platform for machine-learning-enabled multi-agent studies and lays the groundwork for intelligent, adaptive active matter.
item.dc:creator: Isa Mammadli, Prajol Shrestha, Jayant Pande, Filip Novkoski, Siddhant Mohapatra, Martial Noirhomme, Andreas Maier, Nicolas Vandewalle, Ana-Suncana Smith

item.title: Surface Roughness and Filler Restructuring in Magneto-Active Elastomers: Magnetically Hard versus Magnetically Soft Particles
item.description: arXiv:2608.14433v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In magneto-active elastomers (MAEs), a magnetic field reshapes the surface and with it adhesion, friction and wetting. Most use magnetically soft carbonyl iron, whose restructuring has lacked a particle-resolved description. We put forward a molecular dynamics model with magnetizable particles and compare thin layers of hard and soft fillers. Both converge to the same high-field state: a labyrinth of bundled field-aligned chains roughening the surface by about one particle diameter. Hard fillers break and rotate in-plane chains above a threshold field, roughening the surface abruptly. Soft fillers build chains particle by particle, roughening it continuously. The model reproduces the magnetization of carbonyl iron MAEs above about 250 mT and the magnitude of their roughness. Measured roughness varies linearly with inverse zero-field Young's modulus: matrix stiffness, not particle number, controls it. At equal saturation magnetization, filler type sets not how rough the surface becomes, but whether it roughens abruptly or continuously.
item.dc:creator: J\'ulio P. A. Santos, Mehdi Hasanzade, Chaitanya Doifode, Raphael Kriegl, Alexander Kovalev, Mikhail Shamonin, Stanislav N. Gorb, Sofia Kantorovich

item.title: Manufacturing Complex Structures Through Interfacial Self-Organization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09950v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conventional manufacturing constructs three-dimensional geometries through localized material deposition, removal, or shaping, with fabrication effort greatly increasing with geometric complexity. Here, we introduce a manufacturing approach in which target geometry is encoded into sparse wireframe scaffolds that guide liquid self-organization through interfacial forces. We apply a computational framework that approximates arbitrary target geometries using constant-mean-curvature surface domains and extracts their boundaries to construct the scaffolds. Under neutral buoyancy conditions, curable liquids injected into these scaffolds self-organize into the prescribed geometries, which are subsequently solidified into mechanically isotropic structures with optically smooth surfaces. We demonstrate the fabrication of complex anatomical models and topology-optimized structures featuring intricate branching geometries, internal cavities, and integrated materials. This approach opens new possibilities for scalable fabrication of complex geometric designs.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Garrett, Abhinit Sati, Edward Chien, Emily Whiting, Valeri Frumkin

item.title: Catenaries in viscous fluid
item.description: arXiv:1509.01282v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work explores a simple model of a slender, flexible structure in a uniform flow, providing analytical solutions for the translating, axially flowing equilibria of strings subjected to a uniform body force and drag forces linear in the velocities. The classical catenaries are extended to a five-parameter family of curves. A sixth parameter affects the tension in the curves. Generic configurations are planar, represented by a single first order equation for the tangential angle. The effects of varying parameters on representative shapes, orbits in angle-curvature space, and stress distributions are shown. As limiting cases, the solutions include configurations corresponding to "lariat chains" and the towing, reeling, and sedimentation of flexible cables in a highly viscous fluid. Regions of parameter space corresponding to infinitely long, semi-infinite, and finite length curves are delineated. Almost all curves subtend an angle less than $\pi$ radians, but curious special cases with doubled or infinite range occur on the borders between regions. Separate transitions in the tension behavior, and counterintuitive results regarding finite towing tensions for infinitely long cables, are presented. Several physically inspired boundary value problems are solved and discussed.
item.dc:creator: Brato Chakrabarti, J. A. Hanna

item.title: From First Bond to Stable Adhesion: Multivalent Bond Stabilization in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.01293v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: After a particle forms its first receptor--ligand bond near a cell membrane, stable attachment often requires a threshold total bond number $m$. This paper develops a biophysical kinetic theory of this post-capture stage. The bond-number dynamics are modeled as a finite birth--death chain on $n=0,1,\dots,m$, where $0$ is loss of all bonds and $m$ is the stabilization threshold. The mesoscopic rates $\lambda_n$ and $\mu_n$ encode the local energy landscape, accessible receptor--ligand pairs, steric and orientational constraints, and cooperative interactions within the growing cluster. The probability of reaching the threshold before losing all bonds is derived in closed form for general rates and, in the constant-rate case, reduces to a geometric series controlled by the kinetic bias ratio $\rho=\mu/\lambda$. The mean time to failure or stabilization follows from a tridiagonal backward equation. Conditioning on successful attachment is treated as a trajectory-selection effect: the conditioned chain is a Doob $h$-transform whose dissociation rate at $n=1$ vanishes, because successful trajectories cannot lose all bonds before stabilization. A minimal interface between the spatial first-capture probability and the bond-number chain is formulated, together with the conditions under which the stable capture probability factorizes into their product. The analysis shows that hitting probabilities constrain only the rate ratios, whereas the absolute rate scale requires time-resolved or dwell-time data. The threshold $m$ is a model-defined stabilization criterion, not a directly measured ligand count. The rates and threshold are effective parameters specified independently or inferred from kinetic data. The theory provides a quantitative framework for interpreting attachment probabilities, lifetimes, and the transition from first bond formation to a model-defined stabilization threshold.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu

item.title: A unified finite-site framework for scaffold-client biocondensation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15007v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Client recruitment into biomolecular condensates does not determine how stronger binding changes the bulk free-energy advantage of demixing. Here, we use a unified finite-site thermodynamic framework to examine how scaffold-client interactions affect both the response of a fixed-composition mixture and the organization of its ternary phase diagram. The thermodynamic response to increasing client affinity is determined by the difference in heterotypic bonding between the complete equilibrium phase-separated sample and the corresponding homogeneous state. A finite region of the model exhibits positive scaffold-client concentration covariance but negative heterotypic bond contrast: stronger binding reduces the demixing advantage even when both species enrich in the dense phase. This reduction also occurs with independent scaffold self-association and client-binding site pools, without direct displacement of scaffold bonds. A negative response does not by itself imply condensate shrinkage or dissolution. Across composition space, the same finite binding constraints support scaffold-rich and heterotypic coexistence regimes with distinct bond populations. For divalent clients, these regimes can occupy disconnected regions of the phase diagram and reconnect upon increasing client affinity, depending on scaffold cohesion. Critical-point continuation identifies the folds and cusp organizing these changes, while client valence restricts the parameter range over which disconnected coexistence occurs. Explicit-particle Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the qualitative reentrant response and provide finite-size evidence for disconnected coexistence. These results provide a bond-resolved characterization of fixed-parent affinity response and a complementary description of coexistence under specified association constraints.
item.dc:creator: Hamza Coban, Alfredo Alexander-Katz
